contextPassage.title: The Canon and Its Contradictions
contextPassage.text:
The question of how literature acquires cultural clout — how certain works come to be treated as solemn monuments while others dissipate into obscurity — is one that literary historians have long found both pressing and resistant to easy resolution. It is tempting to assert that the answer lies simply in quality; that the works which endure do so because they are, in some objective and impartial sense, the best. But this notion does not survive contact with the actual history of the canon, which is riddled with contradictions that no theory of pure aesthetic merit can plausibly explain.

The processes by which reputations are made and unmade are pervasive and largely invisible. They operate through solicitation and neglect, through the ornate machinery of prizes and syllabuses, through the decisions of editors who conform to the tastes of their moment and critics who tout the fashions of their schools. An author who might have seemed a plausible candidate for lasting prominence in one decade can find herself subordinate to rivals who were, by any dispassionate measure, her inferiors. The indignation such reversals provoke is rarely sufficient to reverse them.

Consider what happens when a discipline is engulfed by a particular doctrine. The consensus that forms around a dominant approach can be immensely productive, but it also tends to impede the kind of wayward thinking from which genuine breakthroughs emerge. The more rigid the hierarchy of approved methods, the more effectively it fetters the imagination of those who work within it. Junior researchers, apprehensive about the prospects for their careers, learn quickly to conform. The result, over time, is a kind of intellectual monotony that no amount of internal debate can fully dispel.

This is not a hypothetical concern. The history of literary criticism is dense with examples of moments when the field became so permeated by a single set of assumptions that alternative conceptions were effectively immured — not banned, but rendered incomprehensible to those who had been trained entirely within the dominant tradition. A subordinate approach might be tolerated, even occasionally celebrated, but only insofar as it did not seriously challenge the doctrine from which the field derived its credibility.

The paradox is that the discipline most devoted to interpreting ambiguity is often the least adept at tolerating it in its own institutional arrangements. Critics who deploy the subtlest tools of close reading in the analysis of a text will bluster past the contradictions in their own methodological premises with a confidence that borders on the irrational. The implication is not that criticism is uniquely dishonest — all disciplines exhibit analogous tendencies — but that the gap between its stated values and its actual practices is particularly apt to go unremarked.

What would a genuinely robust literary culture look like? It would, presumably, cultivate a keen attention to the evidence of the text rather than the reputation of its author. It would treat the notion of a fixed hierarchy of value with the solicitude one extends to a useful but perilous fiction. It would remain perpetually sceptical of the forces — commercial, ideological, sentimental — that attempt to usurp the role of judgement. It would acknowledge, with appropriate severity and without melodrama, that even its most venerated conclusions are provisional.

Such a culture would not be free of discord. Genuine intellectual communities rarely are. The altercation between competing visions of what literature is and does is not a sign of failure but of vitality. What is dismal is not disagreement but the complacent assumption that the current settlement is either impartial or immutable — the nostalgic conviction that the works we now exalt are the ones that simply and obviously deserve it.

The most modest and the most solemn claim that literary criticism can make is also, in the end, its most important: that the task of reading well is never complete, that every confident recount of what a text means is also an invitation to diverge, and that the solitude required to read carefully is not a retreat from the world but the condition under which the world becomes, however briefly and incompletely, comprehensible.
